text.text: Clients ask whether our firmware signing will survive quantum computers — we've been telling them 'we're looking at it' for eighteen months and that answer is wearing thin; we need a concrete migration path to post-quantum algorithms in our HSM product line.

detail.text: Several of our larger clients — two national-level agencies and one payment network operator — have started asking formally, in writing, whether the RSA and ECDSA signing operations inside our KL-HSM line will hold up once capable quantum hardware appears. We first acknowledged the question eighteen months ago and said we were evaluating options. That answer no longer satisfies procurement officers who are planning five- to ten-year infrastructure cycles. We have one engineer who has read the NIST post-quantum standardisation documents and done some prototype work with ML-DSA (formerly Dilithium), but we have not touched the firmware architecture to accommodate larger key material or different signature flows. Our HSM firmware runs on a constrained microcontroller with limited flash and RAM, so a straight drop-in is not possible. We need a migration plan that tells clients which firmware version will support post-quantum algorithms, what the performance trade-offs are, and how hybrid classical/post-quantum operation will work during transition. A good outcome is a documented roadmap and at least one working proof-of-concept integration inside twelve months.

about.text:
Kriptolog a.d. has been building security infrastructure since 1997, when a small team of network engineers in Novi Sad started integrating hardware and software for Yugoslav state institutions. After the turbulent early 2000s, we refocused: instead of reselling other vendors' equipment, we designed our own. Today we develop encryption hardware, public-key infrastructure software, and managed security services used by government agencies, national utilities, and payment processors across the Western Balkans.

Our core product is the KL-HSM line of hardware security modules, manufactured and tested at our facility on the outskirts of Novi Sad. Alongside it, we maintain CertiCore, a certificate issuance and lifecycle management platform that currently issues and tracks roughly 380,000 certificates per year for about a dozen institutional clients. We also offer integration services for customers who need PKI woven into existing identity or payment systems.

The company employs 140 people, roughly half in engineering and the rest split between operations, sales, and support. Our technical leads have backgrounds in cryptographic engineering, embedded systems, and network security. We are not a fast-moving startup; we move deliberately, because the clients who trust us with signing keys and root certificates need exactly that. What sets us apart is that we design, manufacture, and support the full stack — firmware, hardware enclosure, and management software — without outsourcing the sensitive parts.

products.text: KL-HSM hardware security module family (KL-300 and KL-500 series)
CertiCore PKI platform for certificate issuance and lifecycle management
OCSP and CRL responder services for high-availability revocation checking
Managed PKI for government and critical-infrastructure clients

tech.text: Custom ARM Cortex-M firmware in C for HSM cryptographic operations
Java EE backend for CertiCore certificate management platform
PostgreSQL with custom indexing for certificate and revocation databases
Epoxy potting and anti-tamper mesh for HSM physical enclosures
OpenSSL and Bouncy Castle cryptographic libraries
Serbian GAAP accounting, transitioning toward IFRS

plans.text: Kriptolog intends to achieve Common Criteria EAL4+ certification for the KL-500 HSM by the end of 2025 and use that certification as the primary credential for entering German and Austrian government procurement frameworks. In parallel, we plan to release a post-quantum-ready firmware branch for the KL-HSM line and grow the CertiCore platform toward handling one million certificates annually.

rdCapacity.text: We have a core R&D group of twelve engineers working on firmware, cryptographic protocols, and the CertiCore platform, with modest capacity to take on collaborative projects if the scope is well-defined and the output is practically applicable.

pastCollaborations.text: Kriptolog completed a joint testing project with Sigurnost-Pro d.o.o. from Belgrade in 2021, validating interoperability between our OCSP responder and their identity management gateway for a shared government client.
